# Bumpers, sliders and skid plates

> **Some safety-critical values on this page are not confirmed** (marked [Unverified] or [Partial]): they come from one source or are only partly supported. Verify against the factory service manual before use; later runs re-check them against new sources.

> Items marked **[Partial]** are only partly confirmed by the source and need more work. They stay in the review queue and are firmed up, corrected or removed as more sources come in.

## Procedure

> **[Partial]** Needs more work: the verifier could confirm only part of this procedure (the steps marked [Partial], or whether the list is complete). Steps or precautions may be wrong or missing; read the source thread before relying on it. Later runs fill it in as more sources are found.

1. Prime and paint the two metal backing plates.
2. Lay down a carpet on the ground to support the sliders during installation.
3. Place old tackle boxes under the slider assembly to hold it in position.
4. Screw the fine-thread bolt into the threaded hole in the frame.
5. Let that bolt hold up the rear of the slider while you mark the hole.
6. Slide a jack in from the opposite side and jack up the front.
7. Install the front backing plate with its long bolt, tightening just enough to bend the metal slightly.
8. Snug the second bolt at the bottom to secure the alignment.
9. Position the slider so it is parallel to the rocker panel and level from front to rear.
10. Mark the hole location on the frame through the aligned slider.
11. Unless you have a bit of the right size to drill in place, take the slider off before drilling.
12. Drill the marked hole to size with a step drill bit; a right-angle drill helps.
13. Hose down the drilled area with rust converter to prevent internal corrosion.
14. Reinstall all bolts loosely: starting with the rear, then front long, followed by front short.
15. Install the final rear bolt that uses a flat wire loop to seat its nut inside the frame hole.
16. Ease that bolt in and snug it lightly once it catches.
17. Realign all components to ensure the sliders remain level and parallel before fully tightening everything.
18. [Unverified value] Tighten all the bolts down, the wired bolt last; the author used 90 ft Lbs.
19. Tuck the wire loop of the last rear bolt inside the frame to prevent vibration noise.
20. Cut tread tape into shapes and round off all corners for a custom fit.
21. Apply the cut tread tape along the slider edges where tire blast is expected.

_Procedure reported by [t29]; 7 steps reworded by a reviewer. Photos of this job are in the source: <https://www.thenewx.org/threads/how-to-shrockworks-sliders-install-pbr.2743/>_

<details><summary>Alternate procedure [t482] [Partial]</summary>

1. [Partial] Clean the frame thoroughly to remove rust and dirt before installation.
2. [Partial] Disconnect any plastic clips holding wire looms near the mounting area if necessary.
3. Position axle stands or a bottle jack under the rocker panel with the slider resting on top.
4. Align factory holes in the frame so 1/2-inch bolts pass through the mounting plates and frame.
5. [Partial] Thread 1/2-inch x 4-inch bolts with flat washers through front center mounting plates, keeping nuts loose for adjustment.
6. [Partial] Insert a 1/4-inch x 1-1/4-inch backing plate with a welded nut (nut facing away) into the rear slot of the frame bottom and start a 1/2-inch x 2-inch bolt with lock washer and flat washer.
7. [Partial] Push an M12 x 30mm Grade 10.9 bolt through the bottom of the front mounting plate, beginning nuts loosely for adjustment.
8. Adjust slider position front to rear ensuring L-mounting plates sit snug under the frame using a bottle jack if needed.
9. Clamp mounting plates to the frame or tighten bolts in desired positions, positioning C-clamps high on vertical portions to eliminate gaps.
10. Mark hole centers on the underside and face of the frame with a 7/16-inch drill bit by turning it back and forth by hand.
11. Remove the rock slider from the stands to access the marked holes for drilling.
12. Use a center punch and large hammer to pre-punch each mark made by the drill bit.
13. [Partial] Drill pilot holes sequentially with 1/8-inch, then 1/4-inch, and finally 5/16-inch bits while keeping the drill perpendicular to ensure straight bolts.
14. Apply lube during drilling to prevent overheating and breaking the bits.
15. [Partial] Install supplied 3/8-inch x 1-inch thread-cutting bolts using a 9/16-inch socket or air impact wrench, applying significant pressure against the ratchet back.

</details>

10. [Partial] Reach for the interior hatch handle, shut the lid, and verify the installation is complete.

</details>

## Tips & gotchas

- [Partial] Use a step drill bit from Harbor Freight to get the right size without damaging powdercoat. [t29]
- [Partial] Apply tread tape cut into rounded corners on the front square part and first 8 inches of the bottom slider area to prevent tire wear. [t29]
- Use a uni-bit for cleaner hole drilling compared to standard bits. [t29]
- Utilize milk crates as props if jacking up the front end is difficult or impossible. [t29]
- [Partial] Consider adding a tire carrier if you want to move the spare out of harm's way, but ensure it fits in your garage. [t180]
- If using a tire carrier on the driver side, position the hinge close to the trunk so it swings less when opening the hatch. [t180]
- [Partial] Expect to replace bolts as they may strip or require a 'love tap' with a 2lb persuader hammer before installation. [t180]
- [Partial] Use 3/16" steel plate for better bracing if available. [t179]
- [Partial] Alternatively, use two brackets to brace the front section against frame horns. [t179]
- Hold the 550 cord up and slide it between the strap and kit to avoid dangling under the hatch. [t937]
- [Partial] Be careful when unclipping latches so the First Aid Kit doesn't whack you in the head. [t937]
- [Partial] Let it sit longer before unbuckling if stuck. [t937]
- Spray a couple of times previous to unbuckling for stubborn buckles. [t937]
- [Partial] Use a good eye to estimate placement if the area is tight. [t985]
- [Partial] Leave extra material after drilling and clean it up later with sanding bits for better control. [t985]
- Be careful when using the Dremel as it tends to follow its own path. [t985]
- Keep extra bolts on hand for potential future modifications or a second unit. [t283]
- [Partial] Use a flathead screwdriver on the hood strut if applicable. [t479]
- Push against the black plastic at the windshield corner to align the bracket with holes. [t479]
- Use sleeved inserts to snug up front and middle attachments. [t406]
- Note that rear notched holes help address individual frame idiosyncrasies. [t406]
- Use a bottle jack for best results when adjusting the slider position. [t482]
- Keep all 1/2-inch fasteners loose initially to allow full adjustment of the slider. [t482]

## Common mistakes

- [Partial] Overtightening the front long bolt too early, which can bend up the backing plate excessively before alignment. [t29]
- [Partial] Failing to align the slider perfectly parallel to the rocker panel and level from front to rear before drilling. [t29]
- [Partial] Choosing a tight-fitting bumper for 285/75R16 tires without accounting for the spare's location. [t180]
- [Partial] Selecting a tire carrier that leans too far forward, interfering with rear access or garage clearance. [t180]
- Having dirt trapped inside the buckle preventing movement. [t937]
- [Partial] Destroying the template on the first side before repeating it on the other. [t985]
- [Partial] Trapping rust or dirt between sliders and frame during cleaning. [t482]
- Overtightening thread-cutting bolts before threads are fully cut, potentially stripping them. [t482]
